title: Komodo dragons
text:
The Komodo dragon is the largest lizard in the world. A big male can reach about three metres in length and weigh as much as 70 kilograms. Wild dragons live in only a few places, all of them in Indonesia: the islands of Komodo, Rinca and Gili Motang, and some parts of the west coast of Flores.

Komodo dragons are meat eaters. Young dragons spend much of their time in trees, where they catch insects, small lizards and birds. Life up high also keeps them away from adult dragons, which sometimes eat smaller ones. Adults hunt on the ground. They wait quietly beside a trail used by deer or wild pigs, then rush forward in a short burst. Although they look heavy and slow, they can run fast over a short distance.

A dragon finds food mostly by smell. It flicks its long, yellow, forked tongue in and out to collect scent from the air. The tongue carries the scent to a special organ in the roof of the mouth. In this way a dragon can notice a dead animal from a very long way off.

Scientists once believed that germs in the dragon's mouth were the only reason its bite was so dangerous. Newer research shows that dragons also have venom glands in their lower jaws. The venom makes a bitten animal bleed heavily and grow weak, so it cannot escape far.

In 1980, Indonesia created Komodo National Park to protect the dragons. Rangers count the animals regularly and watch for problems such as fires and the hunting of the deer that dragons eat. Visitors must walk with a ranger, who carries a forked stick, because the dragons are wild.

Only a few thousand Komodo dragons remain, and the species is listed as endangered. One reason is that their home is so small. Another is that rising sea levels may flood parts of the low ground where they nest.
